narrationScript: Understanding where to place your JavaScript is crucial for web performance and avoiding errors. This diagram visually compares the impact of two common script placements. On the left, we see what happens when a script is placed in the `<head>` section of your HTML. The browser starts parsing the HTML, but when it encounters the `<script>` tag, it pauses. It must download and execute that JavaScript file completely before it can continue parsing the rest of the HTML. This blocks the rendering of your page, delaying the construction of the DOM, and resulting in a perceived slow page load time for the user. Now, look at the right side, representing the best practice: placing your script just before the closing `</body>` tag. In this scenario, the browser can fully parse and render all of your HTML content first. The entire DOM tree is constructed and ready. Only then does the browser download and execute your JavaScript. This non-blocking approach ensures that users see content quickly, and more importantly, your JavaScript can reliably access and manipulate all the HTML elements, as they are guaranteed to exist in the DOM. This is a key principle for building responsive and error-free web applications.
deliveryNotes: Clearly explain the 'blocking' nature of head scripts
Emphasize the 'non-blocking' benefit of body-end scripts
Connect to user experience and error prevention
